Imagine… the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs simply missed.
Would you even exist?
Sixty-six million years ago, Earth belonged to the dinosaurs.
They had ruled for over one hundred and sixty million years.
Tyrannosaurus hunted in the forests.
Triceratops grazed in herds.
And in the undergrowth, small furry creatures hid in the dark.
Our ancestors.
Most no bigger than a rat.
Then, a new light appeared in the sky.
A rock about ten kilometres wide.
Moving at around twenty kilometres per second.
It was heading for what is now Chicxulub, in Mexico.
Then.
It released more energy than a billion atomic bombs.
It left a crater about one hundred and eighty kilometres wide.
Giant tsunamis raced across the oceans.
Then soot and dust blocked out the Sun… for years.
Food chains collapsed.
About three out of four species disappeared.
Every dinosaur that was not a bird… was gone.
But here is the strange part.
Only about thirteen percent of Earth's surface had rock that could cause this disaster.
A little earlier or later… and it might have hit open ocean.
So let's imagine… it missed.
From here on, this is speculation.
The dinosaurs keep ruling.
And the mammals stay small, hunting insects at night.
In our world, mammals only grew big after the dinosaurs were gone.
Without that space, there might be no whales, no elephants… and no apes.
So would there be humans?
Probably not.
Our species is only about three hundred thousand years old.
The end of a long chain of lucky accidents.
In nineteen eighty-two, one scientist imagined a different thinker.
The dinosauroid.
A big-brained descendant of a clever little dinosaur called Troodon.
Most experts doubt it.
More likely?
Feathered giants in the forests… and tiny mammals at their feet.
No cities.
No lights at night.
But here's the twist.
The dinosaurs never fully disappeared.
The bird on your windowsill… is a dinosaur.
Today, there are more than ten thousand species of them.
The asteroid didn't end the dinosaurs.
It made room for us.
If it had missed… would you rather live in their world?
Or ours?
